title: Radiomap-Assisted Vehicle Trajectory Retrieving in Massive Multiple-Input Multiple-Output (MIMO) Networks
content: The widespread deployment of 5G massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) wireless communication networks has considerably enhanced the utilization of wireless signals for practical vehicle trajectory retrieving (VTR) applications. While angle-based methods can achieve high localization accuracy in line of sight (LOS) environments, they rely on specialized localization receivers installed in vehicles, which increases deployment cost. In contrast, a base station (BS) can estimate uplink channel state information (CSI) from the standard sounding reference signals periodically transmitted by an in-vehicle communication device. These coherent channel estimates can be associated with surveyed positions to construct a radio map and subsequently reused for VTR. However, three challenges remain: 1) full port-domain CSI in a 5G massive MIMO network is high dimensional, making its storage, matching, and spatio-temporal processing costly; 2) identifying a road-constrained trajectory whose radio-map entries match an unlabeled online CSI sequence is difficult; and 3) environmental changes can make a previously surveyed radio map inaccurate. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a segmental vehicle mobility model and a radio map-based trajectory search method, termed RadioVTR. RadioVTR first maps each Nt -dimensional BS-specific static channel to an M-dimensional matching vector and then uses only L selected components from the concatenated MQ-dimensional representation at each time slot. The method performs direct matching in the compressed domain and does not reconstruct the full channel during trajectory retrieval. Furthermore, a radio map adaptation technique is introduced to account for environmental changes using pilot responses. The proposed approach is validated with real measurements from a 5G massive MIMO network in Chengdu, China, and demonstrates superior performance compared with existing methods.
